data.title: UAE says Flydubai suspect intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport
data.description:
The Flydubai co-pilot who attacked the plane’s captain with an axe last month intended to crash the aircraft into a passenger terminal at an Israeli airport, according to authorities in the United Arab Emirates.

The suspect, identified as 29-year-old Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, planned to seize control of the 182-passenger aircraft and crash it into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv to cause mass casualties, the UAE’s top prosecutor said Friday.

In a statement carried by state-run news agency WAM, the official said the assailant carried out the attack “with the intention of causing the greatest possible number of human casualties.”

Authorities said Hammami was inspired by the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the U.S., and had taken two previous flights from Dubai to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the route and airport.

The findings shed new light on the Sept. 30 attack, which forced a FlyDubai passenger plane bound for Israel to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent struggle in the cockpit.

The axe-wielding assailant attacked Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian pilot with 17 years of flying experience, as the aircraft traveled over a region near Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

Despite suffering serious injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene as the plane rapidly lost altitude.

The aircraft plunged an estimated 14,000 to 16,000 feet in less than a minute before passengers were able to restrain the attacker and two reserve pilots took control. The plane safely landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

After receiving treatment from hospitals in Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi, Machchhar later described the struggle during a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

“When I was on the ground, I realized that the aircraft is going down,” Machchhar said in Hindi, according to a translation by The Associated Press. “And I told myself, ‘This is the last push, Smit. The door is right there.’”

Modi praised the captain for preventing what he described as another Sept. 11-style attack, saying he showed “the highest form of courage.”

In Friday’s statement, prosecutors said Hammami confessed to acting alone and provided a detailed account of his preparations and motives in the presence of his lawyer.

data.title: Watch live: Trump takes midterm campaign push to deep-blue New York
data.description:
President Trump will take his midterm message to Syracuse, N.Y., on Friday evening, rallying Republicans as the party looks to flip the governor’s mansion and make gains in next month’s elections.

Trump is expected to campaign alongside GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman, who is looking to unseat Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul in a state where Republicans have struggled to win statewide for decades.

The New York stop is a detour from Trump’s recent swing through red states, where Republicans are scrambling to protect their congressional majorities amid troubling midterm polling.

The president is also expected to make campaign stops in Tennessee, Ohio and Alaska in the coming days. 

The event is scheduled to begin at 7:30 p.m. EDT.

Watch live above.

data.title: Trump sends mixed signals on livestreaming Hasan execution
data.description:
President Trump on Friday seemed undecided on whether the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed like the Pentagon announced.

“Well, they’re making a determination about that, but he will be killed, it will be through firing squad,” Trump told reporters before departing for a rally in Syracuse, N.Y. “He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people and he’s totally nuts.”

“So, I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him,” he continued.

He didn’t answer whether he would watch it. The Pentagon on Thursday said the firing squad execution of Hasan, the convicted Fort Hood, Texas shooter, would be livestreamed on Dec. 3.

It will be the military’s first execution in six decades. The plan to livestream it quickly drew fierce criticism from Republicans and Democrats.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), wrote on the social platform X that he agrees Hasan should face the death penalty, “but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting.”

“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America,” Tillis wrote.

Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Jack Reed (D-R.I.) said in a statement that Hegseth’s plan is “a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters,” and is “absolutely shameful and damaging to America’s interests and core values.”

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood in 2009, killing 13 people.

Vice President Vance told reporters Friday in Lima, Ohio that he wouldn’t be watching the livestream.

“I’ve seen those announcements. I don’t know if that’s actually going to happen,” Vance said.

“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” he continued. “Now that said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”

data.title: Murkowski on public execution: 'I'd expect this from terrorists and dictators'
data.description:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) on Friday urged the Pentagon to reverse its decision to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the convicted Fort Hood shooter.

“There is no need to livestream any execution, including this one,” Murkowski said on the social platform X. “I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America.”

The Alaska Republican argued that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to broadcast Hasan’s death by firing squad would have immense consequences, including bolstering his fame and fulfilling his wish for martyrdom.

“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” she continued. “How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself, so I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision.”

Her remarks add to mounting bipartisan criticism of Hegseth’s plan to publicize Hasan’s execution, scheduled for Dec. 3 at Fort Hood in Texas.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, was convicted in 2013 of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at the military base four years earlier. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death — the first military execution in more than six decades.

During his trial, Hasan reportedly told military mental health workers that he hoped to become a martyr if executed.

Hegseth confirmed Thursday the execution would be open to the public and livestreamed.

“We’ll make sure that the people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” he said.

Murkowski joins GOP Sens. John Curtis (Utah) and Thom Tillis (N.C.) in opposing the broadcast.

Tillis called the plan “beyond disgusting,” while Curtis warned that livestreaming the execution risks turning capital punishment into entertainment.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) also condemned the move, and called for Hegseth’s immediate removal on Friday, comparing the planned broadcast to public executions carried out by U.S. adversaries Iran and the Taliban.

data.title: Trump offers first remarks on Guilfoyle controversy
data.description:
President Trump on Friday reacted to revelations his ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, privately solicited cash to pay down her debts ahead of her confirmation hearing, calling the situation “too bad.” 

The president spoke to reporters outside the White House before departing for a political rally in Alabama. 

“I just heard about it, too bad,” Trump said.

“I don’t know too much but she was always very nice.” 

Trump was responding to a reporter beginning to ask a question, saying, “Have you heard of these reports about your ambassador to Greece,” before being cut off by the president. 

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Guilfoyle had solicited Trump donor Eric Deters to pay her $100,000 credit card bill, sending instructions for a wire transfer that would not leave a paper trail.

“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she wrote on Signal on July 3, 2025, according to messages reviewed by The Hill.

Guilfoyle raised concern that her conversations with Deters would harm her chances at confirmation as ambassador to Greece. Her confirmation hearing took place July 9, 2025. 

In an undated message, Guilfoyle raises concern that discussions with Deters about other payments also would harm her. 

“What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” Guilfoyle’s text read. 

Secretary of State Marco Rubio bristled at reporters’ questions about Guilfoyle’s conduct, while on diplomatic travel to Greece.

The secretary also faced questions about a different Journal report detailing Guilfoyle giving preferential treatment to a lobbyist working for a Greek shipping firm. The Journal report also detailed an episode of Guilfoyle threatening to collapse the Greek government. 

Guilfoyle’s conduct has come under scrutiny from the top Democrats on the foreign affairs panel, who launched investigations after the first Journal report and have expanded their probe following the revelations over the credit card bill. 

“Reports coming out regarding Amb. Guilfoyle’s conduct are deeply concerning and suggest potentially corrupt influences on U.S. foreign policy,” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said in a statement to The Hill.

“I have already demanded answers from Secretary [Marco] Rubio regarding her conduct and will continue to press for transparency and accountability. As I have said before, if these allegations are accurate, Amb. Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position.”

data.title: HHS endorses DEA move to schedule synthetic kratom extracts
data.description:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on Friday added its recommendations to the Drug Enforcement Agency’s (DEA) move to schedule synthetic kratom extracts, putting its support behind the push to regulate the substances colloquially called “gas station opioid.”

In July, the DEA announced plans to temporarily schedule a psychoactive compound derived from kratom called 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and other related compounds as Schedule I, placing it in a category indicating no accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse.

HHS Assistant Secretary for Health Admiral Brian Christine recommended the DEA use concentration or ratio-based thresholds for determining how to schedule synthetically concentrated kratom extracts.

While 7-OH is naturally present in trace amounts in herbal kratom, a plant originating from Southeast Asia, products synthetically concentrating the compound in high amounts have proliferated, becoming readily available in gas stations or tobacco shops.

The department recommended that 7-OH and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI), a related compound, be classified as Schedule I if either compound or a combination of both exceeds “1 milligram per gram in solid powders, encapsulated material, or other solid forms, or exceeds 1 milligram per milliliter in liquid preparations.”

HHS also recommended this classification if the amount of 7-OH, MGPI or a combination of both in a product makes up more than 1 percent of mitragynine, the primary psychoactive alkaloid in kratom that is much milder than the compounds that the DEA and HHS are concerned about.

“Dangerous and addictive opioids do not belong behind convenience store counters,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. “Our nation’s children and communities deserve protection from harmful substances like 7-OH and other powerful synthetic drugs. The actions taken by the Department of Justice today reflect our commitment to keeping Americans safe and holding drug traffickers accountable.”

HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said: “We listened to the public, followed the science, and developed a clear recommended threshold for temporary scheduling that targets concentrated 7-OH and MGPI without sweeping natural botanical kratom into Schedule I. The Trump Administration will continue taking decisive action against dangerous products that fuel addiction while making sure our policies are grounded in rigorous science.”

Fierce, bipartisan pushback over Hegseth’s plan for a livestream execution

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream a military firing squad execution next month is causing a fierce outcry of opposition from both sides of the aisle.

© AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough

The Pentagon on Thursday revealed a surprise plan to livestream the Dec. 3 firing squad execution of the convicted Fort Hood, Texas, shooter, former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, in what would be the military’s first execution in six decades.

 

The plan immediately drew fierce blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers, former Trump administration officials and even the leading Catholic bishop in the U.S., who have called the idea barbaric and below the country’s dignity and standards.

 

Vice President Vance was the first administration official to hint at some unease with the Pentagon’s decision, telling reporters Friday that he will not be watching the execution should it be livestreamed.

And Joe Kent, the former head of the National Counterterrorism Center who resigned in March over the Iran war, said streaming Hasan’s execution is “a stain on our morality.”

 

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood in 2009, killing 13 people. He has never claimed innocence and is set to be put to death on Dec. 3 at 1 p.m. local time at the same military base, according to Hegseth.

data.title: French NBA star Wembanyama expresses support for student protests
data.description:
French-born San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama is expressed support for students in his home country who have taken to the streets in the thousands in recent weeks protesting the conditions of their schools.  

“These are systemic inequalities — problems so deep-rooted ⁠that, in fact, I’m glad that high-school students and young people in general are speaking up,” Wembanyama said in a press conference Thursday, according to online translations. 

“I hear them, and I support them, and ‌I hope the people all over there will do the same,” he added. 

Thousands of French students have taken to the streets since the end of September to protest teacher shortages, building conditions and other problems they say run rampant inside their classrooms.  

The protests have sparked worldwide attention as thousands have been arrested and hundreds injured in the demonstrations. Scores of schools have been damaged or burned.

French officials have tried negotiating with students to no avail, and some have called for parents to be held responsible for any violent acts by the students. 

The debate has made its way to the U.S. as Republicans, including President Trump, blame immigration for the scene in France.  

“What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday.

data.title: International Criminal Court 'firmly rejects' new US sanctions
data.description:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) strongly pushed back on Friday after the U.S. imposed new sanctions on its financial assets, slamming the move as “an assault on the rule of law.”

ICC President Tomoko Akane said in a video shared to the court’s website that it “firmly rejects” the U.S.’s retaliation, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Friday morning as former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded a Nobel Peace Prize. The Trump administration previously sanctioned Akane in August.

Akane called the latest financial penalties an “attack” on the countries that created the ICC and on international legal order. 

“It is an attack on the victims of mass atrocities who have waited years, sometimes decades, for those to be held to account,” she said.

The international judicial body, based in The Hague, Netherlands, was created in 2002 to address global atrocities when countries are unable or fail to intervene.

The ICC has pursued war crimes cases against U.S.-allied Israel over its military offensive in Gaza. Pillay, who received Nobel recognition for her contributions to boosting the impact of international law, recently oversaw a United Nations report that concluded that Israeli forces committed genocide in the region.

In a video shared on social media announcing these sanctions, Rubio cited the court’s efforts to prosecute American citizens, despite the U.S. not being a member of the ICC. 

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us,” Rubio said. “Because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

Rubio also called on U.S. allies who are members of the ICC to “rein in this rogue court.”

Akane said that global leadership must now choose between “a world where might is right” or “a future based on the rule of law.”

“In the face of such attacks, we cannot remain indifferent. All of us, including state parties, have a legal and moral duty to act in defense of the international order,” the judge said. “To stand up for law, not force. We will be judged by history for the choices we make today. 

“I pledge to you: The International Criminal Court will continue its work undeterred, with the firm resolve that justice must prevail,” she continued. 

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also denounced the Trump administration’s sanctions on the ICC as “unacceptable” and called for U.S. to withdraw them in a statement his office released Friday. 

“It is abundantly clear in all the conflicts and crises that plague our world that impunity fuels violence and suffering,” Türk said. “We need to be investing more in ensuring justice and accountability – rather than penalizing those who are documenting, investigating and prosecuting serious violations.”

data.title: Trump confirms he will no longer attend Alabama-Georgia game amid Hurricane Isaias
data.description:
President Trump confirmed that he will no longer attend the University of Georgia vs. University of Alabama game in Tuscaloosa on Saturday as Hurricane Isaias barrels toward the Gulf Coast. 

“Based on the fact that a huge Hurricane/Storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. 

The president added that he hopes the game will go on despite the weather, noting that he will be visiting both teams “at a later date.”

Tuscaloosa is not currently projected to be in the eye of the storm but is under a tropical storm warning. 

The game would have been the second Southeastern Conference (SEC) football game Trump has been to this month. Last month, Trump traveled to Knoxville, Tenn. for the Texas-Tennessee game. 

Trump noted in his post that he is still slated to travel to Clarksville, Tenn. for a rally on Saturday. 

“I will go to Tennessee, where we have quickly called a Big Rally in order to get our fantastic Congressional Candidates, our Great Senator, Bill Hagerty, and a woman who will go down as one of the most impactful Governors in the State’s History, Marsha Blackburn, elected!” Trump said.
